tips.title: Ne and its partner hug the verb
tips.body: Think of the negative as two hands holding the conjugated verb: *ne* on the left, *pas, jamais, rien* or *plus* on the right. In the perfect tense the hands hold the auxiliary, *je n'ai pas fini*, and the participle waits outside.

tips.title: Personne and que break the pattern
tips.body: Two negatives do not sit straight after the verb. *Personne* goes where the person would be, after the participle: *je n'ai vu personne*. *Que* goes right before the thing it limits: *je n'ai vu que le début*.

tips.title: Ne … que means only, not not
tips.body: *Je n'ai que dix euros* is not a negative at all: you have ten euros, and only ten. That is why the article stays: *je n'ai que des devoirs*. In a reading text, look for *que* after *ne* before you decide a sentence says *no*.

tips.title: One negative word per ne
tips.body: *Personne ne* and *rien ne* already hold the negative, so there is no *pas*: *personne n'est venu*. If you see two negative words after one *ne* in your own writing, read it again.

tips.title: Ne pas together before an infinitive
tips.body: When the infinitive is what is negative, keep *ne pas* together in front of it: *j'ai décidé de ne pas continuer*. It saves working out where the two halves would go around a verb that is not conjugated.

why.matters: A negative turns a sentence into its opposite, and in French the meaning often sits in the small second word rather than in *ne*, which speakers drop in conversation. Reading and listening questions in English ask what someone *no longer* does or has *not yet* decided, so *plus*, *jamais* and *pas encore* each point to a different answer. In writing, negatives let you show change and qualify a claim, and every one needs the article after it checked.

examples.title: Je sais pas
examples.body: In everyday speech French people drop the *ne*: *je sais pas*, *j'aime pas ça*, *il y a personne*. Listening texts use natural speech, so the second word, *pas*, *personne* or *jamais*, is the part you actually hear. Written French keeps *ne*, and so should you.

visual.alt: A table comparing spoken French that drops ne with the written form that keeps it

examples.title: Il ne reste plus de places
examples.body: A booking website that says *il ne reste plus de places* is telling you the event is full: *plus* means there are no longer any seats left. *Il ne reste que deux places* means there are still two. One word decides whether you can buy a ticket.

Il ne reste que deux places.

steps.title: The two halves of a negative
steps.body:
A French negative has **two parts**. *Ne* goes **before** the verb and the second word goes **after** it, so the verb sits between them. Before a vowel or a silent *h*, *ne* becomes *n'*.

> *Je **ne** travaille **pas** le samedi.* — I do not work on Saturdays.

Four negatives are on the grammar list for **both tiers**:

- *ne … pas* — not
- *ne … jamais* — never
- *ne … rien* — nothing, not … anything
- *ne … personne* — nobody, not … anyone

> *Je **ne** mange **jamais** à la cantine.* — I never eat in the canteen.
> *Il **ne** fait **rien** le week-end.* — He does nothing at the weekend.
> *Je **ne** connais **personne** dans ma nouvelle classe.* — I do not know anyone in my new class.

A reflexive pronoun stays glued to its verb, so it goes **inside** the two halves: *je **ne** me lève **pas** tôt*.

In conversation French speakers often drop the *ne*: *je sais pas*, *j'aime pas ça*. You will hear that in listening texts, and the second word still carries the meaning. In your own writing, always keep the *ne*.

rows: Je ne travaille pas le samedi.
Je ne mange jamais à la cantine.
Il ne fait rien le week-end.

check.prompt: What does *je ne connais personne dans ma nouvelle classe* mean?
check.solution: *Ne … personne* means **not … anyone**. *Never* would need *jamais*, and *no longer* would need *plus*; the sentence has neither, and it is negative, so *know somebody* is the opposite.

markScheme.description: I do not know anyone in my new class.

options: I do not know anyone in my new class.
I never get to know people in my new class.
I no longer know anybody in my new class.
I know somebody in my new class.

steps.title: Negatives in the perfect tense and with infinitives
steps.body: In the **perfect tense** the auxiliary (*avoir* or *être*) is the verb that gets wrapped. The past participle comes after the second word: > *Je n'ai **pas** fini.* — I have not finished. > *Elle n'est **jamais** allée au Canada.* — She has never been to Canada. > *Nous n'avons **rien** mangé.* — We did not eat anything. **Personne is the exception.** It goes **after the participle**, where the person would go in a positive sentence: > *Je n'ai vu **personne**.* — I did not see anyone. With **a verb plus an infinitive** (*vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, aimer*), wrap the first verb: > *Je **ne** veux **pas** aller à l'université.* — I do not want to go to university. When the **infinitive itself** is negative, both halves go together **in front of it**: > *J'ai décidé de **ne pas** continuer la chimie.* — I decided not to carry on with chemistry. **The article after a negative.** *Un, une, du, de la* and *des* become **de** (or *d'*) after a negative verb: *j'ai **un** stage* becomes *je n'ai **pas de** stage*. Two things stay as they are: *le, la, les* (*je n'aime pas **les** maths*), and anything after *être* (*ce n'est pas **un** problème*).

rows: Elle n'est jamais allée au Canada.
props.title: What changes when you make it negative

visuals.alt: A table of positive sentences beside their negatives, showing the auxiliary wrapped in the perfect, personne after the participle, un becoming de, and les staying the same

check.prompt: Translate into French: **I have never worked.**
check.solution: ***Je n'ai jamais travaillé.*** In the perfect the auxiliary *ai* is wrapped, so *n'* goes before it and *jamais* straight after it, and the participle *travaillé* comes last.

steps.title: Higher tier: plus, que, pas encore, ni … ni
steps.body: Four more negatives are on the **Higher tier** list only (spec page 157). They follow the same sandwich rule, with two twists. - *ne … plus* — no longer, not … any more: *je **ne** fais **plus** de sport.* - *ne … pas encore* — not yet: *je n'ai **pas encore** choisi mes options.* - *ne … que* — only: *je n'ai **que** deux cours le mercredi.* - *ne … ni … ni* — neither … nor: *je n'aime **ni** la physique **ni** la chimie.* **Twist one: ne … que is not really negative.** It means *only*, and *que* goes directly before the thing that is limited, not straight after the verb: *je n'ai vu **que** le début* (I only saw the beginning). Because the meaning is positive, the article does **not** change to *de*: *je n'ai **que des** devoirs de maths.* **Twist two: ni … ni** puts *ni* before each of the two things. The definite article stays (*ni **la** physique ni **la** chimie*), but *un, une, du, de la* and *des* disappear altogether: *je n'ai ni frère ni sœur*. Foundation papers do not test these four; at Higher you need to understand them in reading and listening and use them in speaking and writing.

rows: Je ne fais plus de sport.
Je n'ai ni frère ni sœur.

check.prompt: What does *je n'ai que deux cours le mercredi* mean?
check.solution: *Ne … que* means **only**: two lessons, no more. *Any more* would need *plus*, *yet* would need *pas encore*, and *no lessons at all* would need *pas de cours*.

markScheme.description: I only have two lessons on Wednesdays.

options: I do not have two lessons on Wednesdays any more.
I only have two lessons on Wednesdays.
I have no lessons at all on Wednesdays.
I have not had my two Wednesday lessons yet.

steps.title: When nobody or nothing does the action
steps.body: So far *personne* and *rien* have been the **object**: *je ne vois personne*. They can also be the **subject** of the sentence (Higher tier, spec page 156). Then they come **first**, *ne* follows them, and there is **no pas**: > ***Personne ne** m'a aidé.* — Nobody helped me. > ***Rien ne** change.* — Nothing changes. > *Personne n'aime les examens.* — Nobody likes exams. The commonest mistake is to add *pas* out of habit: *personne n'est pas venu* is wrong, because *personne* is already the negative half. One negative word per *ne*. The verb after *personne ne* and *rien ne* is **singular**, even though *personne* sounds like a crowd: *personne ne **veut** partir*.

props.title: No pas after personne ne or rien ne

visuals.alt: A table of three common mistakes with personne ne and rien ne, the corrected sentence, and the reason

check.solution: ***Personne ne comprend.*** *Personne* is the subject and already the negative half, so there is no *pas*, and the verb is singular: *comprend*, not *comprennent*. *Ne* comes after *personne*, never before it.
options: Personne ne comprend pas.
Personne ne comprennent.
Personne ne comprend.
Ne personne comprend.

steps.title: Making a sentence negative, step by step
steps.body: Work through three checks in order: **find the verb that is conjugated**, **wrap it**, then **check the article**.

visuals.problem: Make negative with ne … plus: *Je fais du théâtre le jeudi.*

steps.text: *Du* comes after a negative verb, so it becomes *de*: *de théâtre*.
steps.note: du, de la, des become de

steps.text: *Je ne fais plus de théâtre le jeudi.* — I no longer do drama on Thursdays.

visuals.problem: Make negative with ne … personne: *J'ai rencontré quelqu'un au stage.*

steps.text: The conjugated verb is the auxiliary *ai*; the participle is *rencontré*.
*Personne* replaces *quelqu'un* and goes where it stood, **after the participle**.
*Je n'ai rencontré personne au stage.* — I did not meet anyone on my work experience.

check.prompt: Make this sentence negative using **ne … plus**: *Je fais du théâtre.*
check.solution: ***Je ne fais plus de théâtre.*** *Ne* before *fais*, *plus* after it, and *du* becomes *de* after the negative verb.

steps.title: À toi : négatifs
steps.body:
Try each one before you look at the table. Say which negative it needs, then write it.

1. I have not yet chosen my options.
2. I only have one sister.
3. Nobody wants to stay at school on Friday afternoon.
4. I have neither a laptop nor a tablet.

For 1, *pas encore* wraps the auxiliary. For 2, *que* goes right before *une sœur*. For 3, *personne* is the subject, so there is no *pas*. For 4, *ni … ni* drops *un* and *une*.

Je n'ai pas encore choisi mes options.

Je n'ai ni ordinateur portable ni tablette.

check.prompt: Translate into French: **I have not yet chosen.**
check.solution: ***Je n'ai pas encore choisi.*** *Pas encore* sits in the same place as *pas*, straight after the auxiliary *ai*, and the participle *choisi* follows.

steps.title: Negatives that carry an argument
steps.body:
In the longer writing tasks a negative does more than say *no*. It lets you **contrast** and **qualify**, which is what an argument needs.

- **Contrast a change over time** with *ne … plus*: *Avant, je voulais être médecin, mais maintenant je ne veux plus faire de longues études.*
- **Limit a claim** with *ne … que*: *Le stage n'a duré qu'une semaine, mais j'ai beaucoup appris.*
- **Reject both options** with *ni … ni*: *Je ne veux ni quitter l'école à seize ans ni aller à l'université tout de suite.*
- **Make a general point** with *personne ne* or *rien ne*: *Rien ne remplace l'expérience.*
- **Say what you did without doing something** with *sans* + infinitive (both tiers): *Je suis parti **sans** dire au revoir.* After *sans* with a noun, leave the article out altogether: *sans problème*, *sans argent*.

Three different negatives in one paragraph, each doing a different job, shows range. Do not force them in where a plain positive sentence says it better.

rows: Je ne veux plus être médecin.
Le stage n'a duré qu'une semaine.
Je ne veux ni partir ni rester.

check.solution: *Le stage n'a duré qu'une semaine* uses *ne … que*: the placement did last, but **only** a week. The sentences with *pas*, *personne* and *plus jamais* all deny something outright.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- *Ne* before the conjugated verb, the second word after it; *n'* before a vowel or silent *h*.
- In the perfect, wrap the auxiliary; *personne* alone goes after the participle.
- Before an infinitive, *ne pas* go together: *de ne pas continuer*.
- After a negative, *un, une, du, de la, des* become *de*; *le, la, les* and anything after *être* stay.
- Higher: *ne … plus* (no longer), *ne … pas encore* (not yet), *ne … que* (only, and no change to *de*), *ne … ni … ni* (neither … nor).
- Higher: *personne ne* and *rien ne* as subject take no *pas* and a singular verb.

rows: ne pas, ne jamais, ne rien, ne personne
ne plus, ne pas encore, ne que, ne ni ni, personne ne, rien ne

questions.prompt: What does *je ne travaille jamais le dimanche* mean?
questions.solution: *Ne … jamais* means **never**. *No longer* would be *ne … plus*, *only* would be *ne … que*, and *this Sunday* would be *ce dimanche*: *le dimanche* means on Sundays in general.
options: I never work on Sundays.
I do not work this Sunday.
I no longer work on Sundays.
I only work on Sundays.

questions.solution: ***Je n'ai rien fait.*** *Rien* sits straight after the auxiliary *ai*, like *pas*, and the participle *fait* comes last.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly says **I do not have a brother**?
questions.solution: ***Je n'ai pas de frère.*** *Ne* and *pas* wrap the verb *ai*, and *un* becomes *de* after a negative verb, so it cannot be left out altogether or moved in front of *pas*.
options: Je n'ai de pas frère.
Je n'ai pas de frère.
Je ne pas ai de frère.
Je n'ai pas frère.

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **I cannot see anyone.** (Use *voir*.)
questions.solution: ***Je ne vois personne.*** *Ne* before *vois*, *personne* after it. In French *I can see* is usually just *je vois*, so no *pouvoir* is needed.

questions.prompt: Make this sentence negative with **ne … pas**: *J'ai trouvé un stage.*
questions.solution: ***Je n'ai pas trouvé de stage.*** The auxiliary *ai* is wrapped, and *un* becomes *de* after the negative verb.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly says **I did not see anyone**?
questions.solution: ***Je n'ai vu personne.*** *Personne* is the one negative that goes **after the participle** in the perfect tense, where *quelqu'un* would stand. It already carries the negative, so there is no *pas*.
options: Je n'ai personne vu.
Je ne personne ai vu.
Je n'ai vu personne.
Je n'ai pas vu personne.

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **I do not want to go to university.**
questions.solution: ***Je ne veux pas aller à l'université.*** The first verb *veux* is wrapped and the infinitive *aller* follows. *Je n'ai pas envie d'aller à l'université* is also right.

questions.prompt: What does *je n'ai pas encore décidé* mean?
questions.solution: *Ne … pas encore* means **not yet**: the decision is still to come. *Never* would need *jamais*, *stopped* would need *plus*, and *only just* would be *je viens de décider*.
options: I have only just decided.
I have never decided anything.
I have stopped deciding.
I have not decided yet.

questions.prompt: Read: *Au collège, on a sept cours par jour, mais le mercredi on n'a que trois cours.* How many lessons are there on Wednesdays?
questions.solution: **3.** *Ne … que* means **only**: on Wednesdays there are only three lessons. The seven is the number on the other days.

questions.prompt: What does *je n'aime ni la physique ni la chimie* mean?
questions.solution: *Ne … ni … ni* rejects **both**: the speaker likes neither subject. Liking one of them would need a *mais*, *no longer* would need *plus*, and *only* would need *que*.

markScheme.description: I like neither physics nor chemistry.

options: I like neither physics nor chemistry.
I like physics but not chemistry.
I no longer like physics or chemistry.
I only like physics and chemistry.

questions.prompt: A student writes *Personne n'est pas venu à la réunion.* What is wrong with it?
questions.solution: *Personne* is the subject here and is already the negative half of *ne … personne*, so *pas* doubles it up. Correct: *Personne n'est venu à la réunion.* *Personne* goes after the participle only when it is the object, and as a subject pronoun it takes no article and a masculine singular agreement.

markScheme.description: The pas must go, because personne is already the negative word.

options: Personne must move after the participle venu.
The pas must go, because personne is already the negative word.
The participle should agree: venue.
Personne needs an article in front of it: la personne.

questions.solution: ***Personne ne m'a aidé.*** *Personne* is the subject, *ne* follows it, and there is no *pas*. *Aidée* is right too if *me* is a girl: the participle agrees with *me*, a direct object before the verb.

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **I no longer have any free time.**
questions.solution: ***Je n'ai plus de temps libre.*** *Ne … plus* wraps *ai*, and *du* becomes *de* after the negative, so *de temps libre*.

markScheme.description: je n'ai plus de temps libre

accepted: je n'ai plus de temps libre

questions.prompt: Which is the correct translation of **I only have one sister**?
questions.solution: ***Je n'ai qu'une sœur.*** *Que* goes directly before the thing that is limited, *une sœur*, and elides to *qu'* before the vowel. *Ne … que* is not really negative, so *une* does not change to *de*. Adding *pas* changes the meaning to *I do not have only one sister*.
options: Je n'ai que de sœur.
Je n'ai pas qu'une sœur.
Je n'ai qu'une sœur.
Je ne qu'ai une sœur.

questions.solution: ***Rien ne change.*** *Rien* is the subject, so it comes first, *ne* follows, and there is no *pas*. The verb is singular.

questions.prompt: What does *je n'ai ni frère ni sœur* mean?
questions.solution: *Ne … ni … ni* rejects both, so the speaker has **no brothers or sisters**. The article *un* or *une* drops out after *ni*, which is why *frère* and *sœur* stand alone. *No longer* would need *plus*, and *only* would need *que*.

markScheme.description: I have no brothers or sisters.

options: I only have a brother and a sister.
I have a brother but no sister.
I no longer have a brother or a sister.
I have no brothers or sisters.

questions.prompt:
Write about 80 words in French about your plans after Year 11. Mention:

- what you do not want to do next year
- something you no longer enjoy at school, and why
- a decision you have not made yet
- what you will do in the summer

Use at least four different negatives.
questions.solution: **Modèle.** > *L'année prochaine, je **ne** veux **pas** quitter l'école, parce que je voudrais étudier les langues au lycée. Je **ne** fais **plus** de physique, car je trouvais les cours trop difficiles et je n'avais **jamais** de bonnes notes. Par contre, je n'ai **pas encore** décidé si je vais continuer le dessin. Rien n'est certain ! Cet été, je vais travailler dans un café, mais je n'aurai **que** deux semaines de vacances.* **What earns the marks.** Six different negatives: *ne pas*, *ne plus*, *ne jamais*, *ne pas encore* in the perfect, *rien ne* as subject, and *ne que*. The article changes after the negatives (*plus de physique*, *jamais de bonnes notes*) but not after *ne … que* (*que deux semaines*), which is not really negative. Present, imperfect, perfect and near future all appear.

de after a negative where needed

questions.prompt:
Translate into French:

1. I do not like chemistry.
2. I never go to the library.
3. I have not found a work placement yet.
4. Nobody wants to leave school at sixteen.
5. I only have two exams next week.
questions.solution:
**Modèle.**

1. *Je n'aime pas la chimie.*
2. *Je ne vais jamais à la bibliothèque.*
3. *Je n'ai pas encore trouvé de stage.*
4. *Personne ne veut quitter l'école à seize ans.*
5. *Je n'ai que deux examens la semaine prochaine.*

**What earns the marks.** Sentence 1 keeps *la* after the negative, because a definite article does not change. Sentence 3 wraps the auxiliary *ai* with *pas encore* and turns *un stage* into *de stage*. Sentence 4 has *personne* as the subject, so there is no *pas*. In sentence 5, *que* goes right before *deux examens*, and nothing changes to *de*, because *ne … que* means *only*. The sentences get harder in order, as the translation on the Higher writing paper does.

examTechnique.body:
In **reading and listening**, find the second half of every negative before you answer. *Plus*, *jamais*, *que* and *pas encore* each give a different answer to a question about what someone does, and in natural speech the *ne* may not be there at all.

In **translation into English**, *ne … que* is *only*, never *not*, and *ne … plus* is *no longer* or *not any more*.

In **writing and translation into French**, check three things for every negative: *ne* before the conjugated verb, the partner in the right place (after the participle for *personne*, before the limited thing for *que*), and *de* in place of *un, une, du, de la, des* after the verb. At Higher tier, use two or three different negatives in a long answer to show control.
examinerErrors: Leaving out *ne* in writing, as speakers do: *je sais pas*.
Putting *pas* after the participle in the perfect: *j'ai fini pas*.
Keeping *un* or *des* after a negative verb: *je n'ai pas un stage*.
Changing the article after *ne … que*, which is not negative: *je n'ai que de devoirs*.
Translating *ne … que* as *not*, which gives the opposite meaning.
Splitting *ne pas* round an infinitive: *de ne continuer pas*.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses negatives to argue, not just to deny. It contrasts past and present with *ne … plus*, limits a claim with *ne … que*, rejects two options at once with *ni … ni*, and makes a general point with *rien ne*. Every negative is placed correctly in the perfect and with infinitives, and the article after it is right. In reading and listening it never misses the difference between *plus*, *jamais*, *que* and *pas encore*.
